newsitem.title: USA: Alaska plans boosted southeast chinook catch.
newsitem.headline: Alaska plans boosted southeast chinook catch.

text.p: Alaska fishermen will be allowed to harvest more than 277,000 chinook salmon in waters of the state's southeast panhandle, thanks to forecasts that show a fish population sharply higher than last year, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game said Wednesday.
The harvest cap was pegged by state biologists and based on a preseason abundance index provided by technical advisers to the Pacific Salmon Commission, state officials said.

The result is a forecasted Alaska harvest of 277,182 of the chinook salmon covered by the Pacific Salmon Treaty, officials said. That compares to a harvest cap of 140,000 to 155,000 treaty chinook salmon last year for southeast Alaska fishermen, said Dave Gaudet, a biologist with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.

The abundance index, 33 percent above base levels measured from 1979 to 1982, reflect growing stocks of salmon spawned on the west coast of Vancouver Island and from the Columbia River basin, Gaudet said Wednesday.
The majority of the southeast Alaska chinook harvest is set to begin July 1, he said.
So far, there has been no adverse reaction from Canadian officials to the increased Alaska harvest forecast, Gaudet said.
The Canadian government, a party to the Pacific Salmon Treaty, has argued that Alaska fishermen intercept too many British Columbia-spawning chinook salmon.

That and other disputes between the Canadians and northwest U.S. states has caused negotiations for a renewed Pacific Salmon Treaty to stall. The 1985 treaty, which allocates portions of the trans-boundary fish between Alaska, British Columbia, Washington and Oregon, has not been renewed since 1994.
